subject: rstan: time and space of different formats on disk

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: rstan: time and space of different formats on disk
parts:
We were discussing the value of compression earlier. I thought a little
test I did might be of interest.

r5 is a stanfit object with results for 3 chains, 2000 iterations each,
c 1600 parameters (though it contains beta and beta_raw for the
normalized and scaled versions of the same parameters). I'm guessing at
the number of parameters.

ls -l r5*
-rw-r--r-- 1 ross ross 2270990496 Sep 19 22:26 r5.rdata.bz2
-rw-r--r-- 1 ross ross 2106135646 Sep 19 21:47 r5.rdata.gz
-rw-r--r-- 1 ross ross 1998663472 Sep 19 22:19 r5.rdata.xz
-rw-r--r-- 1 ross ross 2481455164 Sep 19 21:50 r5-uncompressed.rdata

Times
> save(r5, file="r5.rdata.gz")
# didn't time it, but seemed like several minutes
> system.time(save(r5, file="r5-uncompressed.rdata", compress=FALSE))
user system elapsed
4.425 0.908 27.862
> system.time(save(r5, file="r5.rdata.bz2", compress="bzip2"))
user system elapsed
297.838 2.104 304.288
> system.time(save(r5, file="r5.rdata.xz", compress="xz"))
user system elapsed
1183.858 2.600 1190.272

So compression can save about 1/5 of the space.
Times are on an i5 processor with R 2.15. Also it's an encrypted file
system, but I don't think that affects user time. I used the
development version of stan.

The default behavior seems pretty good; I was surprised gzip did better
than bzip2 (note bzip2 also defaults to a higher compression level). xz
was the most compact, but much slower (20 minutes vs 5 for bzip2 and
probably a bit less for gzip).

The takeaway message seems to be that compression's not worth it.

Encrypting a file system's going to require some overhead, but
I have no idea how it's handled and how well it's pipelined with
the rest of the disk stream.

> I used the
> development version of stan.
>
> The default behavior seems pretty good; I was surprised gzip did better
> than bzip2 (note bzip2 also defaults to a higher compression level). xz
> was the most compact, but much slower (20 minutes vs 5 for bzip2 and
> probably a bit less for gzip).

This data's hard to compress. For example, in natural language text
data, you usually save about 3/4 of the space for English.

It's not that surprising that bzip2 is worse than gzip --- gzip just
uses recent history, whereas bzip builds a suffix array and then compresses
that, which has a high constant overhead.

- Bob
